A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VideoGLaMM work, with matching architecture, equations and original experiments. All supplied pages support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable supplementary Sections A–D.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.4 report original grounded-conversation, visual-grounding and referring-segmentation results, including quantitative ablations and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds Ref-DAVIS-17 and Refer-YouTube-VOS results, further qualitative predictions and video-editing demonstrations.

M1.justification: The core architecture, adapters, losses and training strategy remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds an inference pipeline that supplies VideoGLaMM masks, the source video and an editing prompt to BiVDiff for object removal or replacement. This is a limited procedural extension.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on Ref-DAVIS-17 and Refer-YouTube-VOS, previously identified as training sources, and introduces object-removal and object-replacement demonstrations. These materially broaden evaluation populations and task requirements. Section 5 also stops listing HC-STVG for evaluation, although v1 supplied no corresponding results and both retain it as a dataset-construction source.

E2.justification: The MeViS comparison adds LMPM in Table 2. The new referring-segmentation comparisons introduce LISA-7B/13B and TrackGPT-7B/13B alongside VideoLISA in Tables 3 and 8. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator families; the original GCG and VidSTG comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a two-case qualitative editing test using predicted masks, source videos and editing prompts to condition BiVDiff. Section 5 removes its blanket zero-shot designation and explicitly specifies interrogative VidSTG inputs, although v1 already reported interrogative-only results and v2 retains the introduction's zero-shot claim. No changed training budget, retained metric or existing split is established.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds grounded-conversation and referring-segmentation examples plus two case studies testing whether predicted masks can support video editing. The three controlled analyses of encoder composition, decoder temporal processing and four versus eight frames retain their configurations and numerical results.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional result rows do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched GCG, MeViS, VidSTG and ablation entries are unchanged, but v2 adds two benchmark result sets, the LMPM row and qualitative outcomes. Table 8 reports VideoGLaMM J&F of 66.8 versus VideoLISA's 63.7. Section 5.4 removes the incorrect claim that eight frames improve CIDEr. Table 3 and the added LMPM row contain J/F/J&F inconsistencies, leaving their exact metric assignments uncertain.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same mathematical content; changes are formatting and explanatory wording. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new supplement adds none.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: a dual-encoder grounded video model, the approximately 38k-example annotation benchmark and superior performance across the three principal tasks. The editing application does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 corrects the explanation of decoder supervision by distinguishing input frames from ground-truth masks. Appendix B adds an interpretation of applicability to external video-editing models, while Appendix D introduces licensing, privacy and bias assertions. Existing limitations concerning annotation noise, incomplete object coverage, granularity and video length remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly supplies concrete annotation prompts, worked examples, object-ID and segmentation-tag preservation instructions, and JSON output formats for the three annotation streams. These substantially improve documentation of the existing dataset pipeline without establishing that it changed or was rerun. Backbone, hardware and training-schedule disclosures remain; some dataset-size details are removed from Section 5.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly contrasts the already-cited VideoLISA with VideoGLaMM regarding spatial-only processing and GCG support. BiVDiff and TrackGPT are newly cited works. The additional published Ref-DAVIS reference corresponds to an already-cited work, and the broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording corrections, removes repeated dataset descriptions, adds an equal-contribution note and changes the numbered limitations section into an unnumbered paragraph. Supplementary Sections A–D organize the additions, while the main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual presentation with Tables 3 and 8 and Figures 5–7, including editing sequences and extensive mask-overlaid qualitative panels. Table 2 gains a comparator row; the unchanged Figure 4 and Table 1 are relocated. The architecture and annotation-pipeline graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix C makes the central annotation pipeline more reproducible, while the added evaluations and qualitative examples broaden empirical support. The corrected CIDEr discussion also improves accuracy. These benefits are tempered by newly introduced reporting errors: Table 3 and the LMPM row in Table 2 do not satisfy the stated J&F averaging relationship. The net gain is useful but limited by the reliability of some added comparisons.
